title: Ἔλαφος πηρωθεῖσα
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 105. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔλαφος πηρωθεῖσα τὸν ἕτερον τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν παρεγένετο εἴς τινα αἰγιαλὸν καὶ ἐνταῦθα ἐνέμετο, τὸν μὲν ὁλόκληρον πρὸς τὴν γῆν ἔχουσα καὶ τὴν τῶν κυνηγῶν ἔφοδον παρατηρουμένη, τὸν δὲ πεπηρωμένον πρὸς τὴν θάλασσαν· ἔνθεν γὰρ οὐδένα ὑφωρᾶτο κίνδυνον.
sentences.tr: Elaphos pērōtheisa ton heteron tōn ophthalmōn paregeneto eis tina aigialon kai entautha enemeto, ton men holoklēron pros tēn gēn echousa kai tēn tōn kynēgōn ephodon paratēroumenē, ton de pepērōmenon pros tēn thalassan· enthen gar oudena hyphōrato kindynon.
sentences.l: A deer, maimed in one of her eyes, came to a certain shore and grazed there, holding the sound one toward the land and watching for the hunters' onset, and the maimed one toward the sea; for from that quarter she suspected no danger.
sentences.i: A deer blind in one eye came down to a stretch of shore and grazed there, keeping her good eye toward the land, on the watch for the hunters' approach, and her blind one toward the sea, since from that quarter she suspected no danger.
sentences.n: πηρωθεῖσα τὸν ἕτερον τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν is the accusative of respect: the passive participle says she was disabled, the accusative says in what part — 'maimed as to one of her eyes'. πηρόω is 'cripple, disable' generally rather than 'blind' in particular; with the eye named as the part maimed it comes to the same thing, and the idiomatic line says so. τὸν μέν … τὸν δέ carry ὀφθαλμόν along without repeating it, one eye set against the other as the land is set against the sea. ὑφοράομαι is 'to look at from under', hence to eye with suspicion.

sentences.t: Καὶ δή τινες παραπλέοντες ἐκεῖνον τὸν τόπον καὶ θεασάμενοι αὐτὴν κατηυστόχησαν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē tines parapleontes ekeinon ton topon kai theasamenoi autēn katēustochēsan.
sentences.l: And in fact some men, sailing past that place and catching sight of her, shot her down.
sentences.n: Καὶ δή marks the arrival of just what the last clause had invited. κατευστοχέω is a rare compound of εὖ and στόχος, the aim — 'to hit the mark upon' someone; the augment lengthens the diphthong, κατ-ηυ-.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἐλιποψύχει, εἶπε πρὸς αὐτήν· « Ἀλλ᾽ ἐγὼ ἀθλία, ἥτις τὴν γῆν ὡς ἐπίβουλον φυλαττομένη πολὺ χαλεπωτέραν ἔσχον τὴν θάλασσαν ἐφ᾽ ἣν κατέφυγον. »
sentences.tr: Kai epeidē elipopsychei, eipe pros autēn· « All’ egō athlia, hētis tēn gēn hōs epiboulon phylattomenē poly chalepōteran eschon tēn thalassan eph’ hēn katephygon. »
sentences.l: And when she was fainting away, she said to herself: « Ah, wretched I, who, guarding against the land as treacherous, found the sea far harsher — the sea to which I had fled for refuge. »
sentences.i: And as her life ebbed away she said to herself: « Ah, wretch that I am — I kept my guard on the land as the treacherous side, and the sea I fled to for safety has proved far the crueller. »
sentences.n: Chambry prints πρὸς αὐτήν where the reflexive πρὸς ἑαυτήν is what the sense wants and what the parallel fables write; the meaning is still 'to herself'. λιποψυχέω is 'to leave one's breath behind', to faint away — the imperfect keeps her dying while she speaks. ἥτις introduces the ground of the epithet, exactly as with the deer in the lion's cave. φυλάττομαι in the middle takes the accusative of the thing one is on guard against.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλάκις παρὰ τὴν ἡμετέραν ὑπόληψιν τὰ μὲν χαλεπὰ τῶν πραγμάτων δοκοῦντα εἶναι ὠφέλιμα εὑρίσκεται, τὰ δὲ σωτήρια νομιζόμενα ἐπισφαλῆ.
sentences.tr: Houtō pollakis para tēn hēmeteran hypolēpsin ta men chalepa tōn pragmatōn dokounta einai ōphelima heurisketai, ta de sōtēria nomizomena episphalē.
sentences.l: Thus often, contrary to our supposition, those of things that seem to be harsh are found beneficial, and those thought to be saving, precarious.
sentences.i: Thus often, contrary to what we suppose, the things that look hard turn out to be a help, and the things we count on to save us turn out to be perilous.
sentences.n: ὑπόληψις is the supposition one takes up beforehand; παρά with the accusative of it is 'contrary to' it. The two limbs are balanced by μέν … δέ, and the second has to borrow εὑρίσκεται from the first — Greek leaves it out, English cannot.
